input[type='checkbox'],input[type='radio']{position:absolute;top:0;right:0;bottom:0;left:0;visibility:initial;opacity:0;margin:0;cursor:inherit;padding:0;width:100%;height:100%;}/*!sc*/
input[type='submit']{-webkit-text-decoration:none;text-decoration:none;cursor:pointer;display:inline-block;text-align:center;-webkit-text-decoration:none;text-decoration:none;}/*!sc*/
input[type='submit']:hover,input[type='submit']:focus{-webkit-text-decoration:underline;text-decoration:underline;}/*!sc*/
input[type='reset']{cursor:pointer;}/*!sc*/
input[type='number']::-webkit-inner-spin-button,input[type='number']::-webkit-outer-spin-button{height:auto;}/*!sc*/
input[type='search']{box-sizing:border-box;}/*!sc*/
select{border:1px solid;--border-color__token-name:"colors.interactive.base.black";border-color:rgba(0,0,0,1);padding:0.125em 0.5rem;width:auto;}/*!sc*/
textarea{border:1px solid;--border-color__token-name:"colors.interactive.base.black";border-color:rgba(0,0,0,1);padding:0.125em 0.5rem;display:block;width:100%;max-width:25em;}/*!sc*/
img{max-width:100%;height:auto;vertical-align:bottom;}/*!sc*/
a{cursor:pointer;--color__token-name:"colors.interactive.base.light";color:rgba(223,223,223,1);transition-property:color,background,text-shadow;transition-duration:0.2s;transition-timing-function:ease-in-out;}/*!sc*/
table{width:100%;}/*!sc*/
td{padding:0.5em;vertical-align:bottom;text-align:left;vertical-align:baseline;}/*!sc*/
th{padding:0.5em;vertical-align:bottom;text-align:left;vertical-align:bottom;}/*!sc*/
thead{--border-color__token-name:"colors.foundation.menu.dividers";border-color:rgba(223,223,223,1);border-width:0 0 2px 0;border-style:solid;}/*!sc*/
tfoot{--border-color__token-name:"colors.foundation.menu.dividers";border-color:rgba(223,223,223,1);border-width:2px 0 0 0;border-style:solid;}/*!sc*/
tbody tr{--border-color__token-name:"colors.foundation.menu.dividers";border-color:rgba(223,223,223,1);border-width:0 0 1px 0;border-style:solid;}/*!sc*/
tbody tr:nth-of-type(even){background-color:rgba(
          223,223,223,
          0.5
        );}/*!sc*/
tbody td{--border-color__token-name:"colors.foundation.menu.dividers";border-color:rgba(223,223,223,1);border-width:1px 0 0 0;border-style:solid;}/*!sc*/
tbody td:last-of-type{border-right:0;}/*!sc*/

type="application/ld+json">{"@context":"http://schema.org","@type":"NewsArticle","articleBody":"Stop it, I said in my head. I closed my eyes and tried to calm down by imagining myself as I wanted to be—not the Colorado girl scraping by as a cocktail waitress. My boss, Reardon, a real-estate investor, had decided I would be the hostess of a poker game he had organized at Hollywood’s infamous Viper Room.\n“Molly Bloom, you are wearing the dress of your dreams. You are confident and fearless and you will be perfect.” None of this was true, of course, but I wanted it to be. I opened my eyes, lifted my chin, and relaxed my shoulders. It was showtime.\nThe first person to arrive was Todd, the famous writer and director.\n“Hello,” I said, warmly reaching out my hand. “I’m Molly Bloom.” I gave him a genuine smile.\n“Hi, gorgeous, I’m Todd—nice to meet you in person.\n“Do I give the buy-in to you?” he asked.\n“Sure,” I said, eyeing the giant stack of hundred-dollar bills.\n“Can I get you a drink?” I asked.\nHe ordered a Diet Coke. I went behind the bar and set the enormous amount of money down.\nAfter I served him his drink, I started counting the stack. It was $10,000, all right. I put it in the cash register with Todd’s name on it. I felt cool, edgy, and dangerous counting that much money. The others started to arrive.\nBruce introduced himself and handed me his buy-in as well. I knew from my research that he had been an executive at of one of the most prestigious golf companies in the world. Bob was a real-estate magnate, and Phillip came from a long line of European aristocrats. His mother had been a glamorous supermodel and his father was one of the most famous playboys in Manhattan. Reardon came blasting in with his typical “Oh yeah!” greeting. The rumpled Houston showed up next, followed by Tobey and Leo. I straightened my shoulders and smiled as naturally as I could. They are just people, I told myself as butterflies flew manically around in my stomach. I introduced myself, took their buy-ins, and asked for their drink orders. When I shook Leo’s hand and he gave me a crooked smile from under his hat, my heart raced a little faster. Tobey was cute, too, and he seemed very friendly. I didn’t have any backstory on Houston except that he was somehow involved in the movie business. He had kind eyes, but there was something different about him. He didn’t seem to belong with this crowd. Steve, a major Hollywood director, and Dylan, a producer, showed up next.\nThe energy in the room was palpable. It felt more like a sports arena than the basement of the Viper Room.\nReardon finished ripping into a sandwich and shouted, “Let’s play.”\nI watched, fascinated. It was all incredibly surreal. I was standing in the corner of the Viper Room counting ONE HUNDRED THOUSAND DOLLARS IN CASH! I was in the company of movie stars, important directors, and powerful business tycoons. I felt like Alice tumbling down the rabbit hole.\nAs the players filed out, they thanked me, some kissed my cheek, but they all pressed bills into my hand. I smiled warmly and thanked them in return, trying not to let my hands shake.\nWhen they were all gone, I sat down in a daze, and with trembling hands I counted $3,000.\nHollywooding\n“Whoa, look at you,” the dealer Diego said. “Your tips are going to be good tonight.”\nWhen Tobey and Leo walked in, the guys became a little shy and awkward, except for Reardon, who fist-bumped Leo with a gruff “What’s happening, player?” While the guys clustered around Leo, Tobey went over to Diego and handed him his Shuffle Master. The Shuffle Master is a $17,000 machine that is supposed to deliver a fair, random shuffle every time and increases the speed of each game. Last week, Tobey had told the guys he wouldn’t play without it.\n“Hi, honey,” Bob said now as I took his coat. I saw his eyes flick around the room; even he got a little giddy when he saw that Leo was there. Phillip walked in with his friend Mark. Mark was friends with Pete, a tennis legend, who allegedly played high-stakes poker, too.\nWhen he saw me, Phillip let out a low whistle and kissed my hand.\nI blushed and looked at the floor, enjoying every surreal moment of being the only girl among such handsome, accomplished men.\nAnd then above the buzz of voices came Reardon’s ringing voice.\n“Let’s play!!”\nThey settled into their seats, and the air filled with the smooth sounds of my Frank Sinatra playlist, the whirring of the Shuffle Master, the shuffling of chips, and the happy, playful banter of the players.\nWhen it was time for dinner, I ordered Mr. Chow’s. The guys weren’t thrilled about the idea of stopping the game to eat, and I made a mental note to get side tables and, in the future, let them eat their food at the poker table.\nThe game resumed after dinner at full speed. I sat in the corner, watching Diego’s hands fly around the table pushing chips and flipping cards—it was impossibly hard to keep up with. Suddenly the noise dimmed and Mark stood up. He walked around the table with his hands in his pockets.\nThere was a giant stack of chips in the center. My eyes traced the perimeter of the table to see who still had cards.\nTobey.\nTobey just sat there eating the vegan snack he had brought from home. His round eyes were fixed on Mark.\nMark deliberated while the rest of us held our breath. I had no idea what was happening, but I could feel the suspense.\n“Call!” he announced.\nTobey looked at him in shock.\n“Call?” he asked.\n“Yes,” Mark said. “Do I have you?”\nI tried to add the chips up in my head, but there were so many and they were everywhere.\n“You got me,” Tobey said, and pushed his cards to Diego.\nTobey smiled at Mark. “Nice hand, man.”\nAnd then he looked directly at me, his eyes fixed in a hard stare.\n“Who is this guy?” Tobey texted me.\n“Mark—he’s an attorney.”\n“I see” was all he wrote back.\nI had a sinking sensation that I was now in trouble.\nThe game picked up again, and I held my breath whenever Reardon was in a hand and now Tobey too. I knew Reardon well enough to be certain that the thrill of the game wouldn’t last long if he lost every time. Clearly, I had to keep Tobey happy, too. They both came out ahead, but every second leading up to the last hand of the game was so full of anticipation that by the end of the night I was completely emotionally exhausted. But I loved every minute of it. The game lasted until three A.M.\nAs the guys filed out, I helped them with their coats and valet tickets, air-kissed and/or hugged good-bye, and was handsomely rewarded by each of them with cash or chips. I was immensely appreciative; I felt like it was so much more than I deserved. The biggest tippers were Phillip, Houston, and Bruce, who gave me especially large sums, but I made sure to thank each of them with the same amount of enthusiasm. Tobey, despite being the biggest winner, gave me the smallest tip.\nOnce they were gone, Diego and I sat down at the table. We combined our tips and then counted it out: $15,000. Seventy-five hundred each.\nAt first, the money part stressed me out. I felt bad asking the losers for money, and it took a lot of time to drive all over the city chasing and paying. But I soon came to realize that those one-on-one meet-ups were great opportunities to really get to know the men at the table.\nOn this particular Wednesday, I was scheduled to see Tobey and Phillip.\nI went to Tobey’s first. I was getting used to dropping by there: Tobey won every week.\nI drove slowly up the steep drive, buzzed the security bell, and announced myself. “It’s Molly, dropping off a check.”\nThe long tone indicated that I had clearance. The gates opened slowly and I drove in. At the end of the driveway was Tobey’s palatial house.\nHe was already at the door when I got there. “Heyyyy, how are you?”\n“Hey,” I said, handing him the heavy and awkward Shuffle Master. “Thanks for letting us use this for the game.”\n“No problem,” he said, taking the machine. “I wanted to chat with you about something.”\n“What’s up?”\nHis eyes squinted for a moment. “I think I’m going to start charging rent for the Shuffle Master.”\nI looked past him to the expansive foyer of his mansion in the hills. You could see straight through to the ocean.\nI laughed. Surely he was joking. He couldn’t possibly be serious about charging rent for a machine he insisted that we use, from the guys whose money he was taking every week.\nBut he was as serious as death, and I quickly stopped laughing.\n“O.K.,” I squeaked. “Um, how much?”\n“Two hundred dollars.”\nI smiled to conceal my surprise.\n“I’m sure that will be fine. No problem,” I said.\n“Greeaaat,” he said. “Thanks, Molly. And there’s one other thing. I’d like to know who’s playing every week. I figured this was probably about the hand he had lost to Mark.\n“No problem,” I repeated, wanting out of there before I promised him my firstborn and my soul.\n“All righty, talk to you later,” he said, and waved a cheerful good-bye. The new guy always felt awkward at first, and I tried my best to make him more comfortable. The regulars, especially Todd and Reardon, tried to make him feel uncomfortable. It was like watching a cliquish group of adolescent girls. If the guy started winning off the bat once he sat down, he was picked on even more. If he was losing or playing badly, the guys were much friendlier. If the new player was a celebrity or a billionaire, then all bets were off and he was treated like royalty.\nYou can tell a lot about a man’s character by watching him win or lose money. The higher the stakes, the greater the paranoia.\nI decided to drop Ben’s name in an effort to land Arthur, the ultimate whale.\nI had been doing some checking around about Arthur, who was known for his love of women and his mysterious but ample fortune. I knew that he had more than enough billions to cover his buy-in. I also knew that he loved celebrity and that a superstar actor like Ben was a perfect line to dangle.\n“Hey, Arthur. I’m doing a game for Ben, and we would love it if you played,” I texted.\nWord was out now about the big game, and I had received a few calls from professional poker players practically begging me for a seat. Some offered me straight cash, and some a “free roll,” which means if they won I would get a percentage, and if they lost I wouldn’t have any liability. I knew that letting pros into this game would be a surefire way to lose it. I felt that a huge part of this enterprise depended on discretion, so I tried to discourage spectators when I could, but I couldn’t stop the guys from bringing girlfriends along to show off in front of, or the occasional celebrity from stopping by. Sometimes the rap producer Irv would bring Nelly along. Celebrities were always allowed, to be honest. Like when the Olsen twins showed up with a billionaire I was trying to land for the game. They were in, no questions asked.\nThe final list for the big game was Tobey; Ben; my new whales, Derek and Rick; Bob; Houston; and some new faces: Bosko, a dapper gentleman in his 60s; Mike, a finance whiz who loved to gamble; and Gabe, who back in the day was a television star. All the players except Tobey and Houston were huge action. The going-all-in-blind kind of action. And the initial buy-in was $50,000, which meant there would be half a million dollars on the table before the first cards were dealt. It was going to be a big night.\nThe chemistry at a table is so important. You must start with a carefully balanced mix of personalities. If the balance is off and the stakes are too big for some of the players, it kills the game. Too small and everybody gets bored. The $50,000 buy-in had attracted these guys, and so I knew they could handle it; I also knew that it would create pots big enough to make even the richest guys sweat a little.\nI re-applied my lipstick and waited. I had invited Tiffany and Lauren, new friends I had made during a recent trip to Vegas. The two of them showed up to serve drinks and act as decoration. They looked breathtaking. I knew the guys in the room tonight would have a lot that made them want to stay—on and off the table.\nThe first player to arrive was Derek, who was playing for the first time and had come recommended to me by Blake, a friend in Vegas. “He’s young, rich, and a true degenerate,” Blake had told me. “He’s difficult, but he loses $10 to $20 million a year. Every player that night had done the same—given me a signed check, with the amount left blank to cover his buy-in and his losses if things didn’t go his way. class="has-dropcap body dropcap">At 6:45 P.M. I stood by the front door and waited. I fidgeted with my dress. I started to feel insecure about how to greet the players. I knew their names, but did that mean that I should introduce myself?</p><p>Stop it, I said in my head. I closed my eyes and tried to calm down by imagining myself as I wanted to be—not the Colorado girl scraping by as a cocktail waitress. My boss, Reardon, a real-estate investor, had decided I would be the hostess of a poker game he had organized at Hollywood’s infamous Viper Room.</p><p class="paywall">“Molly Bloom, you are wearing the dress of your dreams. You are confident and fearless and you will be perfect.” None of this was true, of course, but I wanted it to be. I opened my eyes, lifted my chin, and relaxed my shoulders. It was showtime.</p><div class="Container-ioqmpI jzsvml"></div><p class="paywall">The first person to arrive was Todd, the famous writer and director.</p><div class="ConsumerMarketingUnitThemedWrapper-kjbXjp gnOkbl consumer-marketing-unit consumer-marketing-unit--article-mid-content" role="presentation" aria-hidden="true"><div class="consumer-marketing-unit__slot consumer-marketing-unit__slot--article-mid-content consumer-marketing-unit__slot--in-content"></div><div class="journey-unit"></div></div><p class="paywall">“Hello,” I said, warmly reaching out my hand. “I’m Molly Bloom.” I gave him a genuine smile.</p><div class="AdWrapper-fGiLaV icsvgw ad ad--sponsor-product"><div class="ad__slot ad__slot--sponsor-product" data-node-id="9663yl"></div></div><p class="paywall">“Hi, gorgeous, I’m Todd—nice to meet you in person.</p><div class="AdWrapper-fGiLaV icsvgw ad ad--in-content"><div class="ad__slot ad__slot--in-content" data-node-id="yxbr1r"></div></div><p class="paywall">“Do I give the buy-in to you?” he asked.</p><div></div><div></div><p class="paywall">“Sure,” I said, eyeing the giant stack of hundred-dollar bills.</p><p class="paywall">“Can I get you a drink?” I asked.</p><p class="paywall">He ordered a Diet Coke. I went behind the bar and set the enormous amount of money down.</p><p class="paywall">After I served him his drink, I started counting the stack. It was $10,000, all right. I put it in the cash register with Todd’s name on it. I felt cool, edgy, and dangerous counting that much money. The others started to arrive.</p></div></div></div><div class="GridItem-bufwYC fdedvq grid--item grid-layout__aside"></div></div><div class="GridWrapper-uulHE dCnZHU grid grid-margins grid-items-2 ArticlePageChunksGrid-kSknMg gVfIFr grid-layout--adrail narrow wide-adrail" data-journey-hook="grid-wrapper"><div class="GridItem-bufwYC dZtveN grid--item grid-layout__content"><div class="BodyWrapper-cuqCAc dlbacv body body__container article__body" data-journey-hook="client-content" data-testid="BodyWrapper"><div class="body__inner-container"><p class="paywall">Bruce introduced himself and handed me his buy-in as well. I knew from my research that he had been an executive at of one of the most prestigious golf companies in the world. Bob was a real-estate magnate, and Phillip came from a long line of European aristocrats. His mother had been a glamorous supermodel and his father was one of the most famous playboys in Manhattan. Reardon came blasting in with his typical “Oh yeah!” greeting. The rumpled Houston showed up next, followed by Tobey and Leo. I straightened my shoulders and smiled as naturally as I could. They are just people, I told myself as butterflies flew manically around in my stomach. I introduced myself, took their buy-ins, and asked for their drink orders. When I shook Leo’s hand and he gave me a crooked smile from under his hat, my heart raced a little faster. Tobey was cute, too, and he seemed very friendly. I didn’t have any backstory on Houston except that he was somehow involved in the movie business. He had kind eyes, but there was something different about him. He didn’t seem to belong with this crowd. Steve, a major Hollywood director, and Dylan, a producer, showed up next.</p><p class="paywall">The energy in the room was palpable. It felt more like a sports arena than the basement of the Viper Room.</p><p class="paywall">Reardon finished ripping into a sandwich and shouted, “Let’s play.”</p><p class="paywall">I watched, fascinated. It was all incredibly surreal. I was standing in the corner of the Viper Room counting ONE HUNDRED THOUSAND DOLLARS IN CASH! I was in the company of movie stars, important directors, and powerful business tycoons. I felt like Alice tumbling down the rabbit hole.</p><p class="paywall">As the players filed out, they thanked me, some kissed my cheek, but they all pressed bills into my hand. I smiled warmly and thanked them in return, trying not to let my hands shake.</p></div></div></div><div class="GridItem-bufwYC fdedvq grid--item grid-layout__aside"></div></div><div class="GridWrapper-uulHE dCnZHU grid grid-margins grid-items-2 ArticlePageChunksGrid-kSknMg gVfIFr grid-layout--adrail narrow wide-adrail" data-journey-hook="grid-wrapper"><div class="GridItem-bufwYC dZtveN grid--item grid-layout__content"><div class="BodyWrapper-cuqCAc dlbacv body body__container article__body" data-journey-hook="client-content" data-testid="BodyWrapper"><div class="body__inner-container"><p class="paywall">When they were all gone, I sat down in a daze, and with trembling hands I counted $3,000.</p><div role="heading" aria-level="3" class="paywall heading-h3">Hollywooding</div><p class="has-dropcap body dropcap paywall">For the second game, a week later, I showed up in a sexy new dress.</p><p class="paywall">“Whoa, look at you,” the dealer Diego said. “Your tips are going to be good tonight.”</p><p class="paywall">When Tobey and Leo walked in, the guys became a little shy and awkward, except for Reardon, who fist-bumped Leo with a gruff “What’s happening, player?” While the guys clustered around Leo, Tobey went over to Diego and handed him his Shuffle Master. The Shuffle Master is a $17,000 machine that is supposed to deliver a fair, random shuffle every time and increases the speed of each game. Last week, Tobey had told the guys he wouldn’t play without it.</p></div></div></div><div class="GridItem-bufwYC fdedvq grid--item grid-layout__aside"></div></div><div class="GridWrapper-uulHE dCnZHU AssetEmbedCaption-eZIMNW gMgneI asset-embed__caption" data-testid="caption-wrapper"><span class="BaseText-fEwdHD CaptionText-cQpRdU klhnDX hbiMYj caption__text"><p><strong>IN THE CHIPS</strong><br>
Bloom at the Montage Beverly Hills. Photograph by John Russo.</p>
<br></span></div></figure></div><p class="paywall">“Hi, honey,” Bob said now as I took his coat. I saw his eyes flick around the room; even he got a little giddy when he saw that Leo was there. Phillip walked in with his friend Mark. Mark was friends with Pete, a tennis legend, who allegedly played high-stakes poker, too.</p><p class="paywall">When he saw me, Phillip let out a low whistle and kissed my hand.</p><p class="paywall">I blushed and looked at the floor, enjoying every surreal moment of being the only girl among such handsome, accomplished men.</p><p class="paywall">And then above the buzz of voices came Reardon’s ringing voice.</p><p class="paywall">“Let’s play!!”</p></div></div></div><div class="GridItem-bufwYC fdedvq grid--item grid-layout__aside"></div></div><div class="GridWrapper-uulHE dCnZHU grid grid-margins grid-items-2 ArticlePageChunksGrid-kSknMg gVfIFr grid-layout--adrail narrow wide-adrail" data-journey-hook="grid-wrapper"><div class="GridItem-bufwYC dZtveN grid--item grid-layout__content"><div class="BodyWrapper-cuqCAc dlbacv body body__container article__body" data-journey-hook="client-content" data-testid="BodyWrapper"><div class="body__inner-container"><p class="paywall">They settled into their seats, and the air filled with the smooth sounds of my Frank Sinatra playlist, the whirring of the Shuffle Master, the shuffling of chips, and the happy, playful banter of the players.</p><p class="paywall">When it was time for dinner, I ordered Mr. Chow’s. The guys weren’t thrilled about the idea of stopping the game to eat, and I made a mental note to get side tables and, in the future, let them eat their food at the poker table.</p><p class="paywall">The game resumed after dinner at full speed. I sat in the corner, watching Diego’s hands fly around the table pushing chips and flipping cards—it was impossibly hard to keep up with. Suddenly the noise dimmed and Mark stood up. He walked around the table with his hands in his pockets.</p><p class="paywall">There was a giant stack of chips in the center. My eyes traced the perimeter of the table to see who still had cards.</p><p class="paywall">Tobey.</p><p class="paywall">Tobey just sat there eating the vegan snack he had brought from home. His round eyes were fixed on Mark.</p><p class="paywall">Mark deliberated while the rest of us held our breath. I had no idea what was happening, but I could feel the suspense.</p><p class="paywall">“Call!” he announced.</p><p class="paywall">Tobey looked at him in shock.</p><p class="paywall">“Call?” he asked.</p><p class="paywall">“Yes,” Mark said. “Do I have you?”</p><p class="paywall">I tried to add the chips up in my head, but there were so many and they were everywhere.</p><p class="paywall">“You got me,” Tobey said, and pushed his cards to Diego.</p><p class="paywall">Tobey smiled at Mark. “Nice hand, man.”</p><p class="paywall">And then he looked directly at me, his eyes fixed in a hard stare.</p><p class="paywall">“Who is this guy?” Tobey texted me.</p><p class="paywall">“Mark—he’s an attorney.”</p><p class="paywall">“I see” was all he wrote back.</p><p class="paywall">I had a sinking sensation that I was now in trouble.</p><p class="paywall">The game picked up again, and I held my breath whenever Reardon was in a hand and now Tobey too. I knew Reardon well enough to be certain that the thrill of the game wouldn’t last long if he lost every time. Clearly, I had to keep Tobey happy, too. They both came out ahead, but every second leading up to the last hand of the game was so full of anticipation that by the end of the night I was completely emotionally exhausted. But I loved every minute of it. The game lasted until three A.M.</p></div></div></div><div class="GridItem-bufwYC fdedvq grid--item grid-layout__aside"></div></div><div class="GridWrapper-uulHE dCnZHU grid grid-margins grid-items-2 ArticlePageChunksGrid-kSknMg gVfIFr grid-layout--adrail narrow wide-adrail" data-journey-hook="grid-wrapper"><div class="GridItem-bufwYC dZtveN grid--item grid-layout__content"><div class="BodyWrapper-cuqCAc dlbacv body body__container article__body" data-journey-hook="client-content" data-testid="BodyWrapper"><div class="body__inner-container"><p class="paywall">As the guys filed out, I helped them with their coats and valet tickets, air-kissed and/or hugged good-bye, and was handsomely rewarded by each of them with cash or chips. I was immensely appreciative; I felt like it was so much more than I deserved. The biggest tippers were Phillip, Houston, and Bruce, who gave me especially large sums, but I made sure to thank each of them with the same amount of enthusiasm. Tobey, despite being the biggest winner, gave me the smallest tip.</p><p class="paywall">Once they were gone, Diego and I sat down at the table. We combined our tips and then counted it out: $15,000. Seventy-five hundred each.</p><p class="has-dropcap body dropcap paywall">The follow-up to the games was always the same: Organize the players. Pay anyone who had won. Collect from anyone who had lost.</p></div></div></div><div class="GridItem-bufwYC fdedvq grid--item grid-layout__aside"></div></div><div class="GridWrapper-uulHE dCnZHU grid grid-margins grid-items-2 ArticlePageChunksGrid-kSknMg gVfIFr grid-layout--adrail narrow wide-adrail" data-journey-hook="grid-wrapper"><div class="GridItem-bufwYC dZtveN grid--item grid-layout__content"><div class="BodyWrapper-cuqCAc dlbacv body body__container article__body" data-journey-hook="client-content" data-testid="BodyWrapper"><div class="body__inner-container"><p class="paywall">At first, the money part stressed me out. I felt bad asking the losers for money, and it took a lot of time to drive all over the city chasing and paying. But I soon came to realize that those one-on-one meet-ups were great opportunities to really get to know the men at the table.</p><p class="paywall">On this particular Wednesday, I was scheduled to see Tobey and Phillip.</p><p class="paywall">I went to Tobey’s first. I was getting used to dropping by there: Tobey won every week.</p><p class="paywall">I drove slowly up the steep drive, buzzed the security bell, and announced myself. “It’s Molly, dropping off a check.”</p><p class="paywall">The long tone indicated that I had clearance. The gates opened slowly and I drove in. At the end of the driveway was Tobey’s palatial house.</p><p class="paywall">He was already at the door when I got there. “Heyyyy, how are you?”</p><p class="paywall">“Hey,” I said, handing him the heavy and awkward Shuffle Master. “Thanks for letting us use this for the game.”</p><p class="paywall">“No problem,” he said, taking the machine. “I wanted to chat with you about something.”</p><p class="paywall">“What’s up?”</p><p class="paywall">His eyes squinted for a moment. “I think I’m going to start charging rent for the Shuffle Master.”</p><p class="paywall">I looked past him to the expansive foyer of his mansion in the hills. You could see straight through to the ocean.</p><p class="paywall">I laughed. Surely he was joking. He couldn’t possibly be serious about charging rent for a machine he insisted that we use, from the guys whose money he was taking every week.</p><p class="paywall">But he was as serious as death, and I quickly stopped laughing.</p><p class="paywall">“O.K.,” I squeaked. “Um, how much?”</p><p class="paywall">“Two hundred dollars.”</p><p class="paywall">I smiled to conceal my surprise.</p><p class="paywall">“I’m sure that will be fine. No problem,” I said.</p><p class="paywall">“Greeaaat,” he said. “Thanks, Molly. And there’s one other thing. I’d like to know who’s playing every week. If there’s going to be someone new, I would definitely like to know who it is. In advance.” His words came out slowly, sounding soft on the outside but with a sharp-edged threat at the center. I figured this was probably about the hand he had lost to Mark.</p></div></div></div><div class="GridItem-bufwYC fdedvq grid--item grid-layout__aside"></div></div><div class="GridWrapper-uulHE dCnZHU grid grid-margins grid-items-2 ArticlePageChunksGrid-kSknMg gVfIFr grid-layout--adrail narrow wide-adrail" data-journey-hook="grid-wrapper"><div class="GridItem-bufwYC dZtveN grid--item grid-layout__content"><div class="BodyWrapper-cuqCAc dlbacv body body__container article__body" data-journey-hook="client-content" data-testid="BodyWrapper"><div class="body__inner-container"><p class="paywall">“No problem,” I repeated, wanting out of there before I promised him my firstborn and my soul.</p><p class="paywall">“All righty, talk to you later,” he said, and waved a cheerful good-bye. I shook my head as I drove away. I would never understand rich people.</p><div role="heading" aria-level="3" class="paywall heading-h3">Full House</div><p class="has-dropcap body dropcap paywall">After several months I went behind Reardon’s back and plotted with Phillip and Tobey to make the game my own. I thought Reardon would be furious with me, but instead he said, “I’m proud of you. . . . The game is yours. You earned it.”</p><p class="paywall">Part of the fun each week was to bring in a new face. It was kind of interesting to watch the dynamics. The new guy always felt awkward at first, and I tried my best to make him more comfortable. The regulars, especially Todd and Reardon, tried to make him feel uncomfortable. It was like watching a cliquish group of adolescent girls. If the guy started winning off the bat once he sat down, he was picked on even more. If he was losing or playing badly, the guys were much friendlier. If the new player was a celebrity or a billionaire, then all bets were off and he was treated like royalty.</p></div></div></div><div class="GridItem-bufwYC fdedvq grid--item grid-layout__aside"></div></div><div class="GridWrapper-uulHE dCnZHU grid grid-margins grid-items-2 ArticlePageChunksGrid-kSknMg gVfIFr grid-layout--adrail narrow wide-adrail" data-journey-hook="grid-wrapper"><div class="GridItem-bufwYC dZtveN grid--item grid-layout__content"><div class="BodyWrapper-cuqCAc dlbacv body body__container article__body" data-journey-hook="client-content" data-testid="BodyWrapper"><div class="body__inner-container"><p class="paywall">You can tell a lot about a man’s character by watching him win or lose money. Money is the great equalizer.</p><p class="paywall">With the addition of Ben, Derek, and Rick, I had more than enough players for the big game, and I started planning for the following Tuesday at the Beverly Hills Hotel. I asked for Bungalow No. 1 because it was separate from the hotel, impressively appointed, and had a circular foyer that would be useful for keeping the food deliveries and room service separate from the game.</p><p class="paywall">More celebrities and higher stakes meant that ensuring privacy was becoming more and more important. The higher the stakes, the greater the paranoia.</p><p class="paywall">I decided to drop Ben’s name in an effort to land Arthur, the ultimate whale.</p><p class="paywall">I had been doing some checking around about Arthur, who was known for his love of women and his mysterious but ample fortune. I knew that he had more than enough billions to cover his buy-in. I also knew that he loved celebrity and that a superstar actor like Ben was a perfect line to dangle.</p><p class="paywall">“Hey, Arthur. I’m doing a game for Ben, and we would love it if you played,” I texted.</p><p class="paywall">Word was out now about the big game, and I had received a few calls from professional poker players practically begging me for a seat. Some offered me straight cash, and some a “free roll,” which means if they won I would get a percentage, and if they lost I wouldn’t have any liability. I knew that letting pros into this game would be a surefire way to lose it. The pros would win all the money, and part of what made my game so special was the chemistry at the table and the fact that nobody there played poker for a living.</p></div></div></div><div class="GridItem-bufwYC fdedvq grid--item grid-layout__aside"></div></div><div class="GridWrapper-uulHE dCnZHU grid grid-margins grid-items-2 ArticlePageChunksGrid-kSknMg gVfIFr grid-layout--adrail narrow wide-adrail" data-journey-hook="grid-wrapper"><div class="GridItem-bufwYC dZtveN grid--item grid-layout__content"><div class="BodyWrapper-cuqCAc dlbacv body body__container article__body" data-journey-hook="client-content" data-testid="BodyWrapper"><div class="body__inner-container"><p class="paywall">And it wasn’t just that every cardplayer in Hollywood wanted to come to the games; everyone’s friends and their friends wanted to come to watch. I felt that a huge part of this enterprise depended on discretion, so I tried to discourage spectators when I could, but I couldn’t stop the guys from bringing girlfriends along to show off in front of, or the occasional celebrity from stopping by. Sometimes the rap producer Irv would bring Nelly along. Celebrities were always allowed, to be honest. Like when the Olsen twins showed up with a billionaire I was trying to land for the game. They were in, no questions asked.</p><p class="paywall">The final list for the big game was Tobey; Ben; my new whales, Derek and Rick; Bob; Houston; and some new faces: Bosko, a dapper gentleman in his 60s; Mike, a finance whiz who loved to gamble; and Gabe, who back in the day was a television star. All the players except Tobey and Houston were huge action. The going-all-in-blind kind of action. And the initial buy-in was $50,000, which meant there would be half a million dollars on the table before the first cards were dealt. It was going to be a big night.</p><p class="has-dropcap body dropcap paywall">I chose my outfit carefully: a black dress that was just clingy enough to be sexy but not enough to be vulgar. Black Louboutins, Chanel pearls, and a light jacket, which was important because I liked to keep the game room cool. Colder temperatures kept players awake, and there was nothing worse than a tableful of tired, lethargic poker players. I wanted the table exploding with action, energy, and conversation.</p></div></div></div><div class="GridItem-bufwYC fdedvq grid--item grid-layout__aside"></div></div><div class="GridWrapper-uulHE dCnZHU grid grid-margins grid-items-2 ArticlePageChunksGrid-kSknMg gVfIFr grid-layout--adrail narrow wide-adrail" data-journey-hook="grid-wrapper"><div class="GridItem-bufwYC dZtveN grid--item grid-layout__content"><div class="BodyWrapper-cuqCAc dlbacv body body__container article__body" data-journey-hook="client-content" data-testid="BodyWrapper"><div class="body__inner-container"><p class="paywall">The chemistry at a table is so important. You must start with a carefully balanced mix of personalities. If the balance is off and the stakes are too big for some of the players, it kills the game. Too small and everybody gets bored. The $50,000 buy-in had attracted these guys, and so I knew they could handle it; I also knew that it would create pots big enough to make even the richest guys sweat a little.</p><p class="paywall">I re-applied my lipstick and waited. I had invited Tiffany and Lauren, new friends I had made during a recent trip to Vegas. The two of them showed up to serve drinks and act as decoration. They looked breathtaking. I knew the guys in the room tonight would have a lot that made them want to stay—on and off the table.</p><p class="paywall">The first player to arrive was Derek, who was playing for the first time and had come recommended to me by Blake, a friend in Vegas. “He’s young, rich, and a true degenerate,” Blake had told me. “He’s difficult, but he loses $10 to $20 million a year. You want his number.”</p><p class="paywall">Tobey showed up with Houston. Mike showed next. He was a very successful trader who seemed a little ditsy but was a genius with numbers. I’d heard he was an absolute animal at the table, as I found most traders were. He had the same routine of arriving and emptying out his pockets, which always contained a shocking number of items: golf tees, pens, receipts, lip balm. He handed me his blank, signed check, and I clipped it to my board. Every player that night had done the same—given me a signed check, with the amount left blank to cover his buy-in and his losses if things didn’t go his way. For the moment the holding company of Molly Bloom Inc. was officially rich.</p></div></div></div><div class="GridItem-bufwYC fdedvq grid--item grid-layout__aside"></div></div><div class="GridWrapper-uulHE dCnZHU grid grid-margins grid-items-2 ArticlePageChunksGrid-kSknMg gVfIFr grid-layout--adrail narrow wide-adrail" data-journey-hook="grid-wrapper"><div class="GridItem-bufwYC dZtveN grid--item grid-layout__content"><div class="BodyWrapper-cuqCAc dlbacv body body__container article__body" data-journey-hook="client-content" data-testid="BodyWrapper"><div class="body__inner-container"><p class="has-dropcap body dropcap paywall">Mike went to join the other guys, and I motioned Derek over.</p><p class="paywall">He picked up his backpack and followed me into the bedroom, opening the bag as soon as I shut the door. He knew what I wanted: he had $250,000 in cash and another $500,000 in Bellagio chips. As I had explained to him when we met earlier, I couldn’t extend him credit his first time at the game, so by bringing $750,000 he would be able to buy in 15 times that night.</p><p class="paywall">Even though I was tripping on the amount of money I was being given, I smiled as if I did this every day. I didn’t want Derek to start to wonder about the fact that he had just handed three-quarters of a million dollars to a virtual stranger. “Great, I’ll just put it in the safe for now.”</p></div></div></div><div class="GridItem-bufwYC fdedvq grid--item grid-layout__aside"></div></div><div class="GridWrapper-uulHE dCnZHU grid grid-margins grid-items-2 ArticlePageChunksGrid-kSknMg gVfIFr grid-layout--adrail narrow wide-adrail" data-journey-hook="grid-wrapper"><div class="GridItem-bufwYC dZtveN grid--item grid-layout__content"><div class="BodyWrapper-cuqCAc dlbacv body body__container article__body" data-journey-hook="client-content" data-testid="BodyWrapper"><div class="body__inner-container"><p class="paywall">“Don’t run off with it,” he said.</p><p class="paywall">We rejoined the others just in time to see Bosko and Gabe walk in. They gave me a cool hello; they were old-school and I knew it would take some time before they would show me any respect. I didn’t care. My game spoke for itself.</p><p class="paywall">Bob showed up next, and Mike asked me if we could begin.</p><p class="paywall">“Guys, do you want to start?” I asked above the excited banter.</p><p class="paywall">Of course they did.</p><p class="paywall">They drew for seats, and the game was off and running.</p><p class="paywall">In the very first hand, Bob, Bosko, Mike, and Derek were all in. I got the chips and the buy-in board ready. That hand went to Bob, which made both Bob and Diego, whom Bob punished when he lost, very happy.</p><p class="paywall">The guys reloaded, laughing and joking.</p><p class="paywall">“I’ll take 200,” said Mike.</p><p class="paywall">I looked around the room for objections. Mike wanted to make sure he had enough chips to take Bob down.</p><p class="paywall">“Actually,” Mike said, “make it 500.”</p><p class="paywall">I looked at him and he nodded, so I counted $500,000 in chips and gave them to him.</p><p class="paywall">“I’ll take 500, too,” said Derek.</p><p class="paywall">I looked at Tobey at the same moment he looked at me, and nodded to indicate that I had the money in cash. His eyebrows flew up and he looked impressed.</p><p class="paywall">I counted out Derek’s chips.</p><p class="paywall">“Give me 300 more,” Bob said.</p><p class="paywall">Talk about a testosterone contest, I thought, counting out the chips. The cards hadn’t even been dealt for the second hand. As I counted the chips I looked around the table to see if anyone else wanted to play Richest Guy at the Poker Table. With no takers, the action continued.</p><p class="paywall">Just then I got a text from Ben.</p><p class="paywall">“Here,” it said.</p><p class="paywall">A surge of excitement coursed through my body—and in that moment I realized how much I had changed. Ben showing up for my poker game was undeniably monumental, but the butterflies I was feeling now were excitement that he was playing at my table, that he was a part of my game.</p></div></div></div><div class="GridItem-bufwYC fdedvq grid--item grid-layout__aside"></div></div><div class="GridWrapper-uulHE dCnZHU grid grid-margins grid-items-2 ArticlePageChunksGrid-kSknMg gVfIFr grid-layout--adrail narrow wide-adrail" data-journey-hook="grid-wrapper"><div class="GridItem-bufwYC dZtveN grid--item grid-layout__content"><div class="BodyWrapper-cuqCAc dlbacv body body__container article__body" data-journey-hook="client-content" data-testid="BodyWrapper"><div class="body__inner-container"><p class="paywall">I greeted Ben at the door. He was tall and handsome, with a relaxed charisma that not all icons have in person.</p><p class="paywall">He looked surprised when I told him who I was.</p><p class="paywall">“You’re so young,” he said.</p><p class="paywall">“Not that young.” I winked. I was 27, but I looked even younger.</p><p class="paywall">I took his coat and showed him the buy-in sheet.</p><p class="paywall">His eyes flew open and he looked at his watch.</p><p class="paywall">“Two million on the table already?”</p><p class="paywall">“Yep,” I said.</p><p class="paywall">“O.K., give me 50K.”</p><p class="paywall">By now I had learned something about the psychology behind the way a guy asks for chips. Wanting to be overstocked or short-stacked at a table is a clear indication of playing style and ego. Whereas some guys want the tallest piles they can manage, the better to bully the table and scare people, Ben’s buy-in choice told me that he was a smart player who liked to limit his downside, especially at a table with a bunch of guys he wasn’t used to playing with.</p><p class="has-dropcap body dropcap paywall">Rick showed up next. Rick, the videographer, director, and co-star of an infamous sex tape, was crass and dirty, but he was still hot in a caveman kind of way.</p></div></div></div><div class="GridItem-bufwYC fdedvq grid--item grid-layout__aside"></div></div><div class="GridWrapper-uulHE dCnZHU grid grid-margins grid-items-2 ArticlePageChunksGrid-kSknMg gVfIFr grid-layout--adrail narrow wide-adrail" data-journey-hook="grid-wrapper"><div class="GridItem-bufwYC dZtveN grid--item grid-layout__content"><div class="BodyWrapper-cuqCAc dlbacv body body__container article__body" data-journey-hook="client-content" data-testid="BodyWrapper"><div class="body__inner-container"><p class="paywall">I pulled him aside to show him the board.</p><p class="paywall">“Wow, they are swinging, huh?” he said, looking down at me. “Want to fuck?”</p><p class="paywall">I looked back at him, praying my face wasn’t as red as it felt.</p><p class="paywall">“No thanks,” I said as casually as if he had asked me if I wanted a Tic Tac.</p><p class="paywall">He laughed.</p><p class="paywall">“Give me 200K.”</p><p class="paywall">Holy shit. I had a <em>humongous</em> poker game.</p><p class="paywall">As Rick took a seat, I saw him focus on Ben. I saw the wheels turning. Oh God, I thought, don’t let Rick say anything embarrassing. He had no filter.</p><p class="paywall">“Hey, yo, did Jennifer’s ass have cellulite on it, or was it nice?”</p><p class="paywall">The table went silent.</p><p class="paywall">Ben looked at Rick.</p><p class="paywall">“It was nice,” he said, and pushed into a huge pot.</p><p class="paywall">The table laughed and the ice was broken. These may have been larger-than-life characters playing with larger-than-life numbers, but at the end of the day, guys are guys—and strangers quickly became familiar friends at a poker table.</p><p class="paywall">After that uncomfortable moment the game took on a life of its own. It was one of those perfect nights where the conversation was lively, the action was fast and furious, and each one of my usually impossible-to-please players had a look on his face that said he would rather be here, at this table, than anywhere in the world. My tips that night reflected the enormous success of the game. I think I walked away with close to $50,000. I had discovered an incredible niche, and I had learned the formula to make it successful and keep it legal.</p><div role="heading" aria-level="3" class="paywall heading-h3">Ace in the Hole</div><p class="has-dropcap body dropcap paywall">We were at another insane game, and I was watching Guy persuade another player to fold a winning hand. Guy was a huge gambler, aggressive and ruthless at the table. He ran a circus-themed live-performance company that made a billion dollars a year.</p></div></div></div><div class="GridItem-bufwYC fdedvq grid--item grid-layout__aside"></div></div><div class="GridWrapper-uulHE dCnZHU grid grid-margins grid-items-2 ArticlePageChunksGrid-kSknMg gVfIFr grid-layout--adrail narrow wide-adrail" data-journey-hook="grid-wrapper"><div class="GridItem-bufwYC dZtveN grid--item grid-layout__content"><div class="BodyWrapper-cuqCAc dlbacv body body__container article__body" data-journey-hook="client-content" data-testid="BodyWrapper"><div class="body__inner-container"><p class="paywall">Tobey was losing, so he was back to disapproving of me, my tips, and the game in general. Now he was in for $250,000, down to his last $50,000, and trying to dig his way out. Jamie was once again playing like it was his last day on earth, and Tobey knew his best shot at getting out of the hole was Jamie. Pale and thin, Jamie had won $12 million in the World Series of Poker Main Event, the largest sum in the history of the tournament. Usually, I wouldn’t have considered allowing a World Series champion into the game, but Jamie was no pro; he had simply been running hot and playing fearlessly.</p><p class="paywall">Jamie and Tobey were all in, and I wasn’t sure which one I was rooting for. Jamie had almost lost his bankroll, and once he did, I wouldn’t be able to let him play anymore. I liked Jamie—he was kind and generous. Tobey was the worst tipper, the best player, and the absolute worst loser, but I had to worry about my job security if he lost. I held my breath and watched Diego turn over the cards. Tobey won.</p><p class="paywall">Predictably, Tobey stood up immediately after the hand that made him whole. “Well, that’s it for me.” He came over to me and set his stacks on my clipboard.</p><p class="paywall">“Whew, you’re lucky I won that hand,” he said, crinkling his eyes and using his usual half-kidding/half-serious/you-guess-which tone.</p><p class="paywall">I nodded.</p><p class="paywall">“You have to cut Jamie off, you know.”</p><p class="paywall">“I know,” I said, counting Tobey’s chips.</p><p class="paywall">He held a thousand-dollar chip in his hand. He flipped it over a couple times in his fingers.</p><p class="paywall">“This is yours,” he said, holding it out.</p><p class="paywall">“Thanks, Tobey,” I said, reaching my hand out.</p><p class="paywall">He yanked the chip back at the last second.</p></div></div></div><div class="GridItem-bufwYC fdedvq grid--item grid-layout__aside"></div></div><div class="GridWrapper-uulHE dCnZHU grid grid-margins grid-items-2 ArticlePageChunksGrid-kSknMg gVfIFr grid-layout--adrail narrow wide-adrail" data-journey-hook="grid-wrapper"><div class="GridItem-bufwYC dZtveN grid--item grid-layout__content"><div class="BodyWrapper-cuqCAc dlbacv body body__container article__body" data-journey-hook="client-content" data-testid="BodyWrapper"><div class="body__inner-container"><p class="paywall">“If . . . ” he said. “If you do something to earn these thousand dollars.” His voice was loud enough that some of the guys looked up to see what was happening.</p><p class="paywall">I laughed, trying not to show my nerves.</p><p class="paywall">“What do I want you to do?” he said, as if he were pondering.</p><p class="paywall">The whole table was watching us now.</p><p class="paywall">“I know!” he said. “Get up on that desk and bark like a seal.”</p><p class="paywall">I looked at him. His face was lit up like it was Christmas Eve.</p><p class="paywall">“Bark like a seal who wants a fish,” he said.</p><p class="paywall">I laughed again, stalling, hoping he would play the joke out by himself and leave.</p><p class="paywall">“I’m not kidding. What’s wrong? You’re too rich now? You won’t bark for a thousand dollars? Wowwww . . . you must be really rich.”</p><p class="paywall">My face was burning. The room was silent.</p><p class="paywall">“C’mon,” he said, holding the chip above my head. “BARK.”</p><p class="paywall">“No,” I said quietly.</p><p class="paywall">“No?” he asked.</p><p class="paywall">“Tobey,” I said, “I’m not going to bark like a seal. Keep your chip.”</p><p class="paywall">My face was on fire. I knew he would be angry, especially because he had now engaged the whole audience, and I wasn’t playing his game. I was embarrassed, but I was also angry. After all I had done to accommodate this guy, I was also shocked. I had made sure I ran every detail of every game by him, changed the stakes for him, structured tournaments around him, memorized every ingredient in every vegan dish in town for him. He had won millions and millions of dollars at my table, and I had catered to his every need along the way—and now he seemed to want to humiliate me.</p><p class="paywall">He kept pushing it, his voice growing louder and louder. The other guys were starting to look uncomfortable.</p></div></div></div><div class="GridItem-bufwYC fdedvq grid--item grid-layout__aside"></div></div><div class="GridWrapper-uulHE dCnZHU grid grid-margins grid-items-2 ArticlePageChunksGrid-kSknMg gVfIFr grid-layout--adrail narrow wide-adrail" data-journey-hook="grid-wrapper"><div class="GridItem-bufwYC dZtveN grid--item grid-layout__content"><div class="BodyWrapper-cuqCAc dlbacv body body__container article__body" data-journey-hook="client-content" data-testid="BodyWrapper"><div class="body__inner-container"><p class="paywall">“No,” I said, again, willing him to drop it.</p><p class="paywall">He gave me an icy look, dropped the chip on the table, and tried to laugh it off, but he was visibly angry.</p><p class="paywall">When he left, the room was buzzing.</p><p class="paywall">“What was that?”</p><p class="paywall">“So weird.”</p><p class="paywall">“Glad you didn’t do it, Molly.”</p><p class="has-dropcap body dropcap paywall">I knew it was more than a childish tantrum. It had been a challenge because Tobey wanted to show that he was the alpha. I knew I hadn’t made the most strategic decision by refusing to submit, but I also needed to retain the respect of the other players.</p><p class="paywall">For the first time since the game began, I realized that it could end. So, in all likelihood, did Tobey. He had anticipated everything except how much money Diego and I were making, and our take-home seemed to be eating him up.</p><p class="paywall">He began bringing up how much I was making even more frequently, not even trying to hide his dissatisfaction.</p></div></div></div><div class="GridItem-bufwYC fdedvq grid--item grid-layout__aside"></div></div><div class="GridWrapper-uulHE dCnZHU grid grid-margins grid-items-2 ArticlePageChunksGrid-kSknMg gVfIFr grid-layout--adrail narrow wide-adrail" data-journey-hook="grid-wrapper"><div class="GridItem-bufwYC dZtveN grid--item grid-layout__content"><div class="BodyWrapper-cuqCAc dlbacv body body__container article__body" data-journey-hook="client-content" data-testid="BodyWrapper"><div class="body__inner-container"><p class="paywall">“I think the game needs re-structuring,” he said one night.</p><p class="paywall">“How so?”</p><p class="paywall">“Well, you make too much and it takes too long to get paid.”</p><p class="paywall">I raised my eyebrows. In what other universe do you show up, play a game, win a million dollars, and get the check within a week? The only reason this game was still running was that I had searched far and wide to recruit new blood and maintain relationships so that Tobey could take their money. Now he had the balls to suggest that I figure out a way to cap my own salary.</p><p class="paywall">I smiled at him.</p><p class="paywall">“I’ll look into it,” I murmured.</p><p class="paywall">“Thanks,” he said.</p><p class="paywall"><em>Author’s note: In some places, I’ve changed the names, identities, and other specifics of individuals in order to protect their privacy and integrity.
